title: The boulder on the hill
told: a sakhi of Guru Nanak, a traditional story

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when someone pushes you, what do you usually do?
options: honest. then this one is for you. listen.
then this one is for you too. listen.
same for most of us. listen.

steps.line: On a blazing day in the hills, Guru Nanak and his friend Mardana were walking. Mardana was desperately thirsty, and there was no water anywhere.
steps.label: a traditional story

steps.line: At the top of the hill, beside the only spring, sat a Sufi holy man, Wali Qandhari. Mardana climbed up and asked for a drink.
In this telling, he refused: if your master is so great, let him give you water. Three times Mardana climbed, and three times he was turned away.

steps.q: Mardana was turned away again and again. Why did Guru Nanak keep sending him back up, politely?
o: He hoped the holy man would tire of saying no
He gave the holy man every chance to be kind
steps.why: No anger, no threats. Just one more chance, three times over.

steps.q: Mardana comes back with nothing, a third time. What do you think the Guru does?
o: Has Mardana lift a stone where they stand
Climbs the hill to argue with him himself
Leads Mardana on to the next village
steps.why: He didn’t fight for the old spring. He found water right where they stood.

steps.line: The Guru told Mardana to lift a stone at the foot of the hill, and fresh water bubbled up. Up at the top, the old spring began to dry.
The holy man was furious. He pushed a huge boulder down the hill, straight at them.

steps.q: The boulder comes crashing down. What do you think the Guru does?
o: Pushes it back up the hill
Raises one hand and stops it
steps.why: He didn’t run, and he didn’t push it back. Sikhs see both halves of the lesson in that one open hand: no fear, and no hate.

steps.line: Guru Nanak raised his open hand and stopped it. Many Sikhs say his handprint is still in the rock today.

steps.q: Today a gurdwara stands around the rock, in Hasan Abdal, Pakistan. Its name, Panja Sahib, means what?
steps.why: Panja is the palm of the hand. The spring there still flows, and Sikhs travel from all over the world to see it.

steps.line: The Sikh root verse says God is nirbhau, nirvair: without fear, without hate. Sikhs take it as a picture of who a person can become.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Someone at work keeps taking credit for your ideas. What would nirbhau, nirvair look like?
o: Say nothing, to keep the peace
Call them out, loudly, in a meeting
Name it calmly, and hold no grudge
steps.why: Nirbhau: speak up, don’t freeze. Nirvair: no grudge to feed afterward. The boulder stopped, and wasn’t sent back.

say: here’s what i love. the guru didn’t run from the boulder, and he didn’t roll it back. no fear, and no hate either.
the ninth guru, guru tegh bahadur, put it simply: frighten no one, and fear no one. both halves, at once.

steps.q: Mardana, the Guru’s thirsty friend, was a Muslim musician. What did he play while Guru Nanak sang?
o: The tabla, a pair of drums
steps.why: Bhai Mardana played the rabab for Guru Nanak’s hymns through decades on the road. Sikh kirtan, singing the hymns to music, starts with those two.

today.say: today, when someone pushes at you, try both halves: don’t shrink, and don’t push back harder. stand still, and stay kind.
options: nirbhau, nirvair. no fear, no hate.
it is. the guru used one open hand. start small.

Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (Mool Mantar: Nirbhau, Nirvair)

check: The spring, the boulder and the handprint are a traditional miracle story; labeled. Some tellings place it on Guru Nanak’s return from the west.

Wali Qandhari is honored by many Muslims, with a shrine on the hilltop; the lesson calls him “a Sufi holy man” and frames his refusal as “in this telling”. Confirm this framing, and whether to add that many tellings end with him humbled and at peace with the Guru.
